title: What Renovations Add the Most Value to a Flip (And Which Ones to Skip)

sections.content: Every dollar you spend on a flip should work hard for you. The problem is that most investors either over-improve a property for the neighborhood or cut corners on the upgrades that buyers actually care about. Both mistakes kill your margins. Before you swing a hammer, it pays to know exactly what renovations add the most value to a flip — and which ones quietly drain your budget without moving the needle on your after-repair value (ARV). If you want a solid foundation for making these decisions, start with our guide on [How to Analyze Real Estate Deals Like a Pro](aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-deal-analysis). It walks through the full framework for evaluating a deal before you ever commit to a purchase price.
Why Renovation ROI Varies So Much

The return you get from any renovation depends on three things: your market, your price point, and your buyer profile. A granite countertop upgrade in a $150,000 neighborhood in Dallas might return 80 cents on every dollar. That same upgrade in a $500,000 Phoenix suburb could return $1.20 because buyers in that price range expect it. There is no universal renovation playbook. But there are clear patterns across most markets that point to high-value upgrades almost every time.
The best flippers don't ask 'How nice can I make this house?' They ask 'What does a buyer in this zip code expect to pay for?' That shift in thinking is worth tens of thousands of dollars per deal.
The Renovations That Consistently Add the Most Value
1. Kitchen Updates (Budget: $8,000–$25,000 | Typical ROI: 70–100%)

The kitchen sells the house. Study after study shows that buyers make emotional decisions in the kitchen faster than anywhere else. You do not need a full gut renovation. On most mid-range flips, a cosmetic kitchen refresh — new cabinet doors and hardware, resurfaced countertops, updated fixtures, and a new backsplash — costs between $8,000 and $15,000 and can add $20,000 or more to your ARV. If the layout is outdated or appliances are more than 15 years old, budgeting $20,000–$25,000 for a more complete overhaul often makes sense. Stainless steel appliances, soft-close cabinets, and quartz or granite countertops are the three upgrades buyers notice first. Skip custom cabinetry and high-end built-ins unless your comps are above $400,000.
2. Bathroom Remodels (Budget: $5,000–$15,000 per bath | Typical ROI: 60–90%)

After the kitchen, bathrooms drive buyer decisions more than any other room. Dated tile, pink fixtures, and worn vanities signal that the house has been neglected — even if everything else is updated. A full primary bathroom remodel in a median price home typically runs $10,000–$15,000 and can add $15,000–$20,000 to your sale price. Secondary bathrooms respond well to lighter refreshes: a new vanity, updated light fixture, new toilet, and retiled floor can cost as little as $3,000–$5,000 and add meaningful value. Double vanities are popular in primary baths right now, especially in markets like [Phoenix](aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) and [Las Vegas](aiwholesail.com/markets/las-vegas-nv) where buyer expectations skew higher.
3. Curb Appeal and Exterior (Budget: $3,000–$10,000 | Typical ROI: 75–150%)

You cannot sell a house that buyers will not walk into. Curb appeal is your first impression and it is heavily underinvested on most flips. Fresh exterior paint or a power wash, new front door, updated house numbers, landscape cleanup, and mulch can cost $3,000–$6,000 total and make a massive difference in how quickly the house sells and for how much. In competitive markets like [Dallas](aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), a home with strong curb appeal can sell 20–30% faster than a comparable property that looks neglected from the street. Faster sales mean less holding cost, which directly improves your net profit.
4. Flooring Replacement (Budget: $4,000–$12,000 | Typical ROI: 80–100%)

Old carpet, cracked tile, and worn hardwood are deal killers. New flooring throughout a home reads as clean and move-in ready — exactly what buyers want. Luxury vinyl plank (LVP) flooring has become the go-to choice for flippers because it is durable, water-resistant, looks like real hardwood, and typically costs $2.50–$4.50 per square foot installed. A 1,500-square-foot home can get all new LVP flooring for $5,000–$8,000. That investment almost always comes back at closing and often returns more than it costs.
5. Fresh Paint (Budget: $2,500–$6,000 | Typical ROI: 100–150%)

Interior and exterior paint is the highest ROI renovation on almost any flip, full stop. A full interior repaint in neutral tones — think warm greiges, soft whites, and light grays — costs $2,500–$4,000 for a 1,500–2,000 square foot home when you use a professional crew. It makes everything look cleaner, larger, and newer. Never skip this one. It is the best money you will spend on a flip.

Pro Tip: Stick to one or two neutral paint colors throughout the entire house. Consistent color palettes photograph better, feel more cohesive during showings, and appeal to a wider range of buyers. Sherwin-Williams Accessible Beige, Agreeable Gray, and White Duck are popular flip favorites that work in most light conditions.
Renovations That Often Cost More Than They Return

items: Swimming pools: Costs $30,000–$60,000 to install, adds far less to ARV in most markets, and can actually deter buyers with families or buyers concerned about maintenance costs.
Luxury appliances: Sub-Zero refrigerators and Wolf ranges make sense above $600,000. Below that, buyers will not pay extra for the brand name.
Sunrooms and room additions: Permits, structural work, and HVAC extensions make additions expensive. They rarely return dollar for dollar unless the home is undersized for the neighborhood.
Over-the-top landscaping: Basic cleanup and fresh mulch, yes. Elaborate stone patios, water features, and mature tree installations, no.
High-end light fixtures: Buyers notice lighting but they do not pay for designer brands. Clean, modern, budget-friendly fixtures from a big box store photograph just as well.

sections.content: How to Build a Renovation Budget That Actually Works

The most common mistake investors make is estimating renovations from memory or gut feeling. Accurate numbers require a scope of work with line-item costs for every task. If you have never built one before, our [Scope of Work Template for Rehab Projects](aiwholesail.com/blog/scope-of-work-template-rehab) gives you a ready-to-use framework. Once you have your scope, cross-check your numbers against realistic cost ranges for your market. Our article on [How to Estimate Rehab Costs for Investment Properties](aiwholesail.com/blog/how-to-estimate-rehab-costs) breaks down costs room by room so you have a benchmark to work from.

It also helps to understand where most investors go wrong at a higher level. The [Fix and Flip Cost Breakdown: What Investors Get Wrong](aiwholesail.com/blog/fix-and-flip-cost-breakdown) article covers the hidden costs — permits, holding costs, carrying charges, closing costs — that eat into profits even when the renovation itself goes smoothly. If you are newer to the process, our [Real Estate Investing for Beginners](aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) guide is a great place to build your foundational knowledge before your first flip.

Pro Tip: Always add a 10–15% contingency buffer to your renovation budget. Surprises are not a possibility on a flip — they are a certainty. Hidden water damage, outdated electrical panels, and permitting delays are the three most common cost blowouts. Budget for them in advance so they do not wreck your projected profit.
Prioritizing Your Renovation List: A Simple Framework

When you are building your renovation plan, rank every item in one of three buckets. First, required repairs: anything structural, mechanical, or safety-related that a buyer's inspector will flag and a lender will require before funding. These include roof repairs, HVAC systems, electrical panels, and plumbing. These come first, no exceptions. Second, high-ROI cosmetic upgrades: kitchen, bathrooms, paint, flooring, and curb appeal. These come second and represent the bulk of your value-add budget. Third, optional enhancements: things like smart home features, epoxy garage floors, or outdoor living spaces. These come last and only get funded if your budget allows after the first two categories are covered.
A good renovation budget is not about spending as much as possible. It is about spending the right amount in the right places to hit your ARV target and leave room for profit.

Before you finalize any renovation budget, run your numbers through a reliable estimating tool.
